new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemically significant: a heavy stress falls automatically on the first syllable of the word unit, and other syllables take a weaker level of stress.
new_statements.citation: Newman, Stanley. 1996. Sketch of the Zuni Language. In Ives Goddard (ed.), Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 17: Languages, 483-506. Washington, D.C.: Smithsonian Institution.

The excerpt is HNAI pp. 485-486 only (page numbers 485 and 486 appear in the text; closing line cit…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog StressTyp2 record gives Zuni initial stress (initial stress); Newman states exactly initial, automatic, non-phonemic stress. Also supplies the 'not phonemically significant' qualification and the domain ('word unit').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and fully automatic: primary (heavy) stress on the first syllable of the word unit; all other syllables carry weaker stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only 'other syllables take a weaker level of stress'; no explicit secondary-stress pattern (no alternation stated). Vowel section adds that short vowels gain slight length in the initial open syllable of a word and that /i/ may be laxer 'in weak-stressed syllables'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Zuni proper (Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico); no dialect specified. Newman's data go back to his 1958 dictionary and 1965 grammar; Miner explicitly relies on Newman and on Bunzel's 1932 texts rather than new fieldwork. The Miner copy opened is the 1983 KWPL working-paper version of the 1986 IJAL article.

new_statements.quote: p. 84: "For reasons which will become clear, I write the wholly predictable word stress (the first syllable of a word is stressed). It is written in Bunzel's texts so I am not supplying anything; however I have not done any new fieldwork on Zuni at this writing." p. 85: "The nouns arising from this type of compounding are unit nouns and like all Zuni lexical words carry a single primary stress on their first syllable: tátepowanne etc."

Note: the DOI 10.17161/kwpl.1808.479 resolves to the 1983 Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics 8(2): 83-93 working-paper version of the paper, not the 1986 IJAL article; same author/title/topic, pagination differs. Stress facts are taken from Newman (NG = Newman 1965) and Bunzel's texts, not new fieldwork.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is wholly predictable: every lexical word carries a single primary stress on its first syllable. True compounds (first member reduced to C(C)V) are one word with one initial stress; 'nominal # nominal' and stripped/loosely-incorporated noun-verb constructions keep two stresses, one per member, which Miner uses as the criterion that the members are separate words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'a single primary stress' per lexical word.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the rule itself; the paper uses retained separate stresses to diagnose loose incorporation vs. true compounding (pp. 85-91).

The Miner copy opened is the 1983 KWPL working-paper version of the 1986 IJAL article.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict initial (word domain) rests on Newman 1965:14, held as PDF+scanned and confirmed verbatim at section 1.5 p.14; StressTyp2 (Miner 1986:245) says the same; Bunzel 1933-38 p.435, downloaded now from archive.org, independently states 'The primary accent is always on the first syllable' (with secondary accent on penult/antepenult in 5+-syllable words, matching Newman's subphonemic secondary stress, and a compound exception where a monosyllabic first stem yields primary accent on the second syllable -- a refinement worth a caution note, not a reclassify, since Newman's later phonemic analysis assigns strong stress to the first syllable of every word unit). No instrumental study or contrary description was found (Crossref search of IJAL and general queries; Suggested action: promote Newman 1965:14 into the empty quote/cite/loc/grade fields as t

sources.quote: "1.5. Stress. The position of the strong stress is morphologically determinable, for this stress falls on the first syllable of the word unit. All other syllables have the weak stress. ... In words of four syllables or more, a subphonemic secondary stress may sometimes be heard on the penult or antepenult, occurring as a fluctuating phenomenon. When it appears, it is considerably weaker in articulatory force than the strong stress." (Newman 1965:14)

sources.quote: p.435 section 10: 'The Zuni language has clearly marked and characteristic stress accent. The primary accent is always on the first syllable. Words of five or more syllables have a secondary accent, usually on the penult, occasionally on the antepenult, but never on the final syllable, except for a rhetorical accent in the imperative and optative.' Section 11 (p.435-436): 'Compounds retain the original stem accents ... In compounds of which the first part is a monosyllabic stem, followed by a polysyllabic stem or stem plus suffixes, the two stems are accented, the primary accent being on the s
sources.locator: sections 10-11 'Accent and Quantity', p.435-436 (TOC: '10. Rules of accentuation 435'; running head '436 BUNZEL ZUNI' follows section 11)
